title: Split a Network into Two Teams
statement:
There are n people, numbered 0 to n − 1. graph[i] lists the people who have a conflict with person i. Conflicts go both ways: if j is in graph[i], then i is in graph[j]. Nobody conflicts with themselves, and no pair is listed twice.

Can you split everyone into two teams so that every conflict is between people on different teams? Return true or false.

The network may come in several separate pieces, and some people may have no conflicts at all.

examples.why: The conflicts form a square 0–1–2–3–0. Teams {0, 2} and {1, 3} work.
A triangle: once 0 and 1 are on different teams, 2 conflicts with both of them.
The pair 0–1 splits fine, but people 2, 3, 4 form a separate triangle. Starting a search only from person 0 never sees it.

constraints: graph[i] has no duplicates and does not contain i
j in graph[i] if and only if i in graph[j]
hints: Pick anyone and put them on team A. Where must each of their conflicts go? And the conflicts of those?
Once one person's team is fixed, the whole connected piece around them is forced. You only need to check that the forced choices never contradict each other.

BFS from every person who has no team yet, giving each neighbour the opposite team. If a neighbour already has the same team as the current person, return false. Restarting from every unvisited person covers separate pieces.

explain.intuition:
In a connected piece there is no real choice. Put the first person on team 0; their neighbours must be on team 1, those neighbours' neighbours on team 0, and so on. So coloring with BFS or DFS either finishes without a clash, or finds a conflict between two people who were forced onto the same team. A clash happens exactly when the piece has a cycle of odd length, like the triangle.

Two details matter. The network can be in several pieces, so start a new search from every person who has no team yet. People with no conflicts are trivially fine. A union-find version also works: all of one person's neighbours must end up on the same team, so union them together, and fail if a person ever lands in the same set as one of their neighbours.
steps: Create team, an array of −1 (no team yet).
For each person s with team[s] == −1, set team[s] = 0 and push s on a queue.
Pop u. For each neighbour v: if team[v] == −1, set team[v] = 1 − team[u] and enqueue it; if team[v] == team[u], return false.
When every piece is colored without a clash, return true.
pitfalls: Searching only from person 0. The third example hides its triangle in a separate piece.
Marking a person as visited without a team value, then skipping them later. You need the team to detect a clash, not just a visited flag.
Using recursion on a long chain of 10 000 people. Python's default recursion limit is 1000; use an explicit queue or stack.

solutions.title: BFS two-coloring
solutions.idea: Color every unvisited person 0 and spread alternating colors through their piece. A neighbour with the same color is a contradiction.

solutions.title: Union-find on neighbours
solutions.idea: All of a person's conflicts must share one team, so union them. A person in the same set as one of their conflicts means no split exists.

followups: When the answer is false, return an odd cycle as proof. How do you recover it from the BFS?
Conflicts arrive one at a time and you must say after each one whether a split is still possible. Which structure handles that? (Hint: union-find that also tracks parity.)
